new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Malto. A syllable containing a long vowel is always stressed e.g. qēn 'guiltless'. In two consecutive syllables when both have long vowels then the last one is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Das, Sisir Kumar. 1973. Structure of Malto. Annamalainagar: Annamalai University.
new_statements.locator: p.34, section 1.6 'Stress' (PDF page 44 of the archive.org scan)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; it is attracted to long vowels (a long-vowel syllable is stressed), and where two adjacent syllables both have long vowels the second (rightmost) carries the stress. No default position is stated for words with only short vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source does not say where stress falls in all-short-vowel words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology chapter (after intonation contours); based on Sauria-side Malto speech (Sahibganj/Godda/Hiranpur informants). The author regards Kumarbhagi as a barely distinct dialect but gives it only a lexical appendix, so application to kuma1274 is by extension, not direct observation. The kmj-specific grammar (Mahapatra 1979) notes only that vowel length is distinctive in the word-initial syllable and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog splits Malto into Kumarbhag Paharia (kuma1274/kmj, the southern/'non-beef-eating' Malto of Pakur-Godda, incl. Mahapatra's 'Malpaharia dialect of Malto') and Sauria Paharia (saur1249/mjt). The only opened source with a stress statement, Das 1973, describes Malto from Sauria-side speakers (Hiranpur/Banjhi schools, main informant from Kusumghati, Godda) and treats 'Kumarbhagi' only in a two-page appendix (word list, no prosody), while asserting 'the difference between the two is very little.. mutually understandable' (p.4) and that he 'did not notice any difference in the phonology and morphology of Malto spoken in different areas' (p.7 of intro). So the quoted statement is first-hand for Malto as a whole but its evidential base is saur1249, not kuma1274; the kmj-specific grammar (Mahapatra 1979, Malpaharia dialect) is silent on stress. Cataloguing Das under kuma1274 would count one description across two glottocodes; a sibling check folder (saur1249) already holds Das 1973.

new_statements.quote: There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: CUP. Ch.2 'Phonology: descriptive' (suprasegmentals).
new_statements.locator: Book p. 27, sec. 1.5.1 'Phonology' (PDF p. 30 of the ch. 1 file; quote verified on the page image). Sec. 2.4.1 'Stress and intonation' (p. 58 by TOC) exists but is not held by the project; seen only as Google Books snippets.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for kuma1274; the existing statement is Das 1973 (Malto-specific, weight-sensitive: a long-vowel syllable is always stressed, and of two consecutive long syllables the last is stressed). Krishnamurti 2003 agrees that stress is non-phonemic but gives a different default placement: initial syllable 'short or long', with non-initial long vowels merely 'louder'. For a word with a short initial and a long non-initial vowel the two rules put primary stress on different syllables (initial vs the long syllable). Soft conflict: Krishnamurti's sentence is a family-wide typological summary that does not cite any Malto data, and his own caveat (non-initial long vowels louder)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide generalization, not a Malto-specific description: stress is non-phonemic in every Dravidian language; by default the first syllable of the word carries stress (loudness) whether short or long; any non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. The Malto entry on the same page (no. 25, 'Malto (Rajmahali, Maleri)') gives only population, location and the references Droese 1884 and Mahapatra 1979, nothing on stress. Sec. 2.4.1 'Stress and intonation' (p. 58) opens 'Very little has been written about stress and intonation' (Google Books snippet); Malto+stress/stressed/accent/loudness/intonation snippet queries surfaced no Malto-specific stress sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated in the text read (sec. 1.5.1). Sec. 2.4.1 not read in full.
new_statements.exceptions: 'A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (p. 27) - a weight caveat on the initial-stress default; 'Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost' (p. 28).
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti 2003 treats 'Malto (Rajmahali, Maleri)' as one language (entry no. 25, p. 27; refs Droese 1884, Mahapatra 1979) and makes no Kumarbhag/Sauria distinction; the stress sentence is family-wide, not tied to any Malto variety. The existing Das 1973 statement is, per the folder's, based on Sauria-side Malto (Hiranpur, Banjhi, Godda informants), with Kumarbhagi only in an appendix word list; so no source held by the project describes Kumarbhag Paharia stress specifically.

readall_conflicts: Das 1973 (Malto-specific, existing statement: stress non-phonemic; a syllable with a long vowel is always stressed; of two consecutive long syllables the last is stressed) vs Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27 (family-wide: no phonemic stress in any Dravidian language; stress normally on the initial syllable, short or long; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels). Both agree stress is non-contrastive. They differ on default placement in words with a short initial and a long non-initial vowel: Das puts stress on the long syllable, Krishnamurti keeps it initial and calls the long vowel only 'louder'. Krishnamurti's sentence is a typological generalization over the whole family with no Malto evidence cited, and his loudness caveat covers the Das observation, so the disagreement is one of labelling more than of substance; Das remains the only Malto-specific statement.
